name: Amplitude
tagline: Build a bounded event explorer for funnels, cohorts, and retention on one product

pricing.notes: Typical Plus monthly entry package; usage terms apply.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 2,000,000 events/month; 10,000 session replays/month; 2,000 AI feedback records; 500 active AI Visibility prompts; unlimited seats
tiers.notes: Permanent free plan; no credit card.

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: First 2,000,000 events/month free; scales to 70,000,000 events; 20 behavioral cohorts; 1,000 active AI Visibility prompts; 2-year retention
tiers.notes: Usage-based after the included 2M events. Exact price depends on event volume; official 5M-event example is $561/month on monthly billing or $5,388/year ($449/month equivalent).

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: Custom event volume; 20,000 session replays/month; 2,500 active AI Visibility prompts; SSO and project permissions

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom event volume; 50,000 session replays/month; 5,000 active AI Visibility prompts; unlimited projects per portfolio

pricing.freeTierCaps: 2,000,000 events/month, 10,000 session replays/month, 2,000 AI feedback records, 500 active AI Visibility prompts, and unlimited seats
pricing.billingTerms: Plus is usage-based with monthly and annual billing; first 2M events/month are $0; Growth and Enterprise are custom contracts
pricing.hiddenCosts: Plus becomes usage-priced above 2M events/month. Growth/Enterprise product expansions and add-ons are priced as a percentage of the platform plan.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Amplitude, build a bounded event explorer for funnels, cohorts, and retention on one product. The hard boundary is behavioral data platform, experimentation, identity, governance, and scale, plus data pipeline reliability and analytical depth.
coreLoopDIY: Collect privacy-conscious first-party events, answer a small set of product questions with funnels, cohorts, and retention views, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
whatYouLose: behavioral data platform, experimentation, identity, governance, and scale
moatNotes: data pipeline reliability and analytical depth
ongoingBurden: event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Amplitude because teams pay because analytics must keep collecting and remain trustworthy while the product changes underneath it. The recurring cost buys event schemas, bot filtering, identity, late data, retention, query cost, privacy, backups, and always-on ingestion, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Umami
priorArt.desc: Popular open-source privacy-focused web analytics platform.

alternatives.name: Mixpanel Free
alternatives.desc: The same class of explorer for free, capped at a million events and five saved reports per seat.

facts.install: Create a hosted project and add a Mixpanel SDK or tracking snippet
facts.dataFormat: Structured events and user profiles are stored in Mixpanel's managed cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan's event, saved-report and advanced-feature limits constrain sustained team use, and its experimentation and governance are less deep than Amplitude's.
facts.setupBlocker: The software installs cleanly, but meaningful use starts with designing an event taxonomy and instrumenting the product

alternatives.name: OpenPanel
alternatives.desc: Mixpanel's useful bits, plus a ClickHouse stack you now get to know personally.

facts.install: Create a hosted account or run the self-host installer and Docker stack
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment uses PostgreSQL for account data, ClickHouse for event data and Redis for cache and queues; hosted data lives in OpenPanel's service
facts.gapVsPaid: Its behavioral analysis, experimentation, taxonomy management and data governance are less deep and mature than Amplitude's.
facts.setupBlocker: None for the hosted free tier; self-hosting requires Docker, DNS or a reverse proxy and several persistent services

alternatives.name: PostHog
alternatives.desc: Funnels, cohorts and retention on a free million-event allowance; the kitchen sink comes along.

facts.install: Create a PostHog Cloud project or use the hobby self-host script on a Linux server
facts.dataFormat: The self-hosted stack splits analytics, transactions, queues and recordings across ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis and object storage; cloud data lives in PostHog's managed regions
facts.gapVsPaid: Its kitchen-sink product is heavier, while Amplitude's core product-analytics workflows and governance are more refined.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting is an unsupported, resource-heavy multi-service stack requiring serious operations work

alternatives.name: Umami
alternatives.desc: Funnels, cohorts and retention without turning the analytics stack into a second product.

facts.install: Create an Umami Cloud account or deploy the Node application with Docker Compose and PostgreSQL
facts.dataFormat: A self-hosted deployment stores analytics and account data in PostgreSQL; Umami Cloud stores it in Umami's managed service
facts.gapVsPaid: It is far shallower for cohorts, retention, experimentation, taxonomy governance and behavioral analysis than Amplitude.
facts.setupBlocker: None for hosted signup; self-hosting requires Docker or Node hosting and a PostgreSQL database

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Plus plan and a single-product first-party analytics DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Amplitude in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: collect privacy-conscious first-party events, answer a small set of product questions with funnels, cohorts, and retention views, and retain raw data under the owner's control.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Ship a lightweight browser SDK for page views and explicit custom events.
Create projects, API keys, environments, event names, and a documented event schema.
Ingest idempotently, filter obvious bots, truncate IP data, and avoid fingerprinting.
Build dashboards for visitors, sessions, funnels, retention, sources, pages, and events.
Expose filters by date, environment, device, country, referrer, and selected properties.
Add retention controls, raw-event export, deletion, health checks, and backup instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out cross-site identity graphs.
Deliberately leave out session replay and automatic DOM capture.
Deliberately leave out warehouse-scale reverse ETL and enterprise governance.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
